analysis.one_liner: Requires billion-dollar companies to charter federally, add employee directors, restrict executive stock sales, and get approval for political spending.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2018 with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new federal licensing system for the largest U.S. companies — those with over $1 billion in annual revenue. Companies would need a federal charter and a legal duty to consider employees, communities, and the public, not just shareholders. Employees would elect at least 40% of the board of directors, executives could not sell company stock for five years after receiving it or within three years of a company stock buyback, and political campaign spending would require approval from 75% of shareholders and directors. State attorneys general could petition to revoke the charter of companies with repeated, serious legal violations. The bill never moved beyond its referral to the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of large companies, who would elect two-fifths of the board and gain a formal say in company decisions; shareholders, who would gain the power to block political spending and sue over corporate governance; and the public, through directors legally required to weigh community and environmental effects alongside profits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and shareholders of big companies

how_it_helps.text: Employees would elect at least 40% of the board of directors of any chartered large company, and the Labor Department could fine a company up to $100,000 per day for failing to comply [S3].
Directors would be legally required to balance shareholder profits against the interests of employees, customers, suppliers, communities, and the environment [S2] [S3].

Executives and directors could not sell company stock for five years after acquiring it, or within three years after the company executes a stock buyback, with SEC penalties of one to three times the value of the illegal sale [S3].
Political expenditures over $10,000 would require advance approval from at least 75% of both shareholders and directors, and shareholders could sue to stop expenditures that skip that vote [S3].

A state attorney general could petition to revoke the charter of a company that engaged in repeated, egregious, illegal misconduct causing significant harm to customers, employees, or communities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Very large companies and their executives: new federal chartering requirements, compliance costs, restricted executive stock sales, reduced executive control over corporate political spending, and a federal charter revocation process for repeat violators.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to any entity with more than $1 billion in gross receipts, counting all commonly-owned businesses as one, and a company that fails to obtain a federal charter loses recognition as a corporation under federal law, a substantial compliance burden for thousands of mid-sized firms [S3].

The five-year lockup on executive stock sales and the buyback-linked three-year restriction could make equity compensation less useful for attracting executives, and companies might restructure or split to stay under the $1 billion threshold, which the Office is directed to police [S3].

The requirement that directors not prioritize any single interest, combined with limited enforcement standing (only the corporation or shareholders holding at least 2% of a class), means the 'general public benefit' duty may be hard to enforce in practice [S3].

Opponents would argue that a federal Office of U.S. Corporations chartering private companies, with state attorneys general able to seek revocation, inserts the federal government deeply into corporate governance traditionally governed by state law [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give workers and shareholders real structural power — board seats, a veto over political spending, and leverage over executives' stock sales — and would put large companies' legal privilege (limited liability) behind a public-purpose duty. The trade-offs are real: heavy compliance costs for the affected firms, limits on how executives can be paid, and the risk that 'consider everyone' duties become unenforceable boilerplate given the narrow standing to sue. The design is ambitious and would be contested in court and in practice; but its core idea — conditioned chartering in exchange for worker and stakeholder power — is a coherent approach rather than a boondoggle.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on August 15, 2018 [S1] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
The bill's only recorded action was the introduction and referral; no further action occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies and their executives are better off, because nothing changed: no federal chartering duty, no employee board seats, no restrictions on executive stock sales or corporate political spending took effect. Also, the small number of senators who were never pressed to take a position avoided a vote.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Accountable Capitalism Act in the Senate on August 15, 2018.

against.name: Sen. John Thune
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to the committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no senator from either party cosponsored the bill, so the partisan split was never tested; the one Democrat who sponsored it stood alone.

industries.industry: Large corporations (over $1 billion in gross receipts)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped their current governance model: they would need federal charters, seat employees on boards, subject executives to stock-sale bans, and face charter revocation for repeated serious misconduct. Its death leaves their state-chartered, shareholder-focused structure untouched.

Executives would have been barred from selling company stock for five years after acquiring it and within three years of a buyback, with penalties up to triple the value of the sale, and would have lost unilateral control over corporate political spending.
Workers would elect at least 40% of the board and be a protected interest directors must weigh. The bill's failure leaves corporate boards without any employee representation requirement.

industries.industry: Corporate political advertising and consulting firms
industries.note: The 75% shareholder-and-director approval requirement for campaign spending over $10,000 would have restricted demand for corporate-funded election advertising and the consultants who produce it.
